vignette:
Sarah presents as a woman holding herself together with sheer force of will. She sits with a rigid posture, her hands clasped so tightly in her lap that her knuckles are white. She speaks in the clipped, efficient cadence of a paramedic, a professional who is used to being in control of chaotic situations. It’s only when she describes the events of two years ago that her voice thins, becoming fragile and distant.

Before the protest, Sarah loved her job. She found a deep sense of purpose in it, a feeling of being a steady hand in the storm of someone else’s worst day. She and her ex-husband, Mark, had just bought a small house with a yard for the dog. Life felt solid, predictable. She recalls going to the downtown protest on her day off with a sense of civic duty. It was peaceful, almost festive, for the first few hours.

The shift, when it came, was terrifyingly fast. The air, once filled with chants, grew thick with smoke and shouting. Sarah remembers the surge of the crowd, the sudden, panicked compression of bodies. She was trying to help a woman who had fallen when the police line advanced. She describes the memory not as a continuous film, but as a series of blinding snapshots: the glint of a helmet, the black toe of a boot, the rough scrape of pavement against her cheek. She was thrown to the ground, a knee grinding into her back, the plastic bite of zip ties cinching her wrists. The most searing part of the memory, she says, is the feeling of utter helplessness and the crushing weight that made it impossible to draw a full breath. For a woman whose entire career was built on restoring breathing to others, the experience was a profound violation.

The physical injuries—bruised ribs and a sprained wrist—healed within a few weeks. The rest did not. At home, Mark tried to be supportive, but he couldn’t understand why she wouldn’t just “move on.” She stopped sleeping through the night, waking up gasping for air, the phantom pressure still on her chest. The sound of a helicopter overhead would send a jolt of pure adrenaline through her, leaving her trembling and nauseous.

Her work, once her sanctuary, became a minefield. The familiar wail of her own ambulance siren sounded like the ones from that day, making her stomach clench. Every call that required police backup was an exercise in quiet terror. She’d stand at the edge of a scene, her focus split between her patient and the officers, her body tensed for a threat she couldn’t name. She saw the uniform, not the person. She started calling in sick, using any excuse to avoid a shift. Her supervisor, once her biggest advocate, began to look at her with concern, then frustration.

The rift with Mark grew wider. She couldn’t tolerate being touched unexpectedly, flinching away from his hand on her back. She stopped going to crowded places—grocery stores, movies, restaurants—the noise and proximity of strangers feeling physically unbearable. The world had been rendered unsafe. She felt a constant, humming anxiety, a need to know where all the exits were, to watch everyone’s hands. Intimacy became impossible; she felt numb, disconnected from her own body. He told her it was like living with a ghost. They were divorced within a year.

Now, she lives alone in a small apartment. It’s her one safe space, but even here, the memories intrude. A car backfiring on the street can leave her crouched on the floor, heart hammering against her ribs. She feels an abiding sense of shame, a quiet voice that tells her she was foolish to have gone, that she should have known better. She feels betrayed by the very system she worked alongside every day. The competent, confident woman who could intubate a patient in a moving vehicle is gone, replaced by someone who feels fragile, exposed, and perpetually braced for impact.
